name: Acadesine
lead: Acadesine, also called AICAR or AICA riboside, is a nucleoside that activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses cellular energy status.[3][1] It was studied clinically for protecting the heart during surgery and in some blood cancers, and in 2008 a mouse study described it as an exercise mimetic, which led to interest from athletes and in online fat-loss and performance discussions.[2][1]
Human data for appearance or body-composition purposes are absent. The World Anti-Doping Agency has listed acadesine as a prohibited substance since 2009.[1]

paras: AICAR is taken up by cells and converted to a monophosphate that mimics AMP, activating AMPK.[3] In rat muscle, it increased AMPK activity, fatty acid oxidation and glucose uptake.[5] Activation of AMPK has also been reported to suppress muscle protein synthesis signaling via mTOR.[9]

Acadesine was first explored in the 1980s to preserve blood flow to the heart during surgery, and was developed by PeriCor Therapeutics and licensed to Schering-Plough in 2007. A phase III heart-surgery trial began enrolling in 2009 and was stopped in 2010 after an interim futility analysis.[1] In 2008 a Cell paper reported that AICAR improved endurance in sedentary mice, describing AMPK activators as exercise mimetics.[2]

Registered trials include a small 2002 trial of exercise-mediated glucose uptake in type 2 diabetes (n=40)[11] and a 1996 pilot study in two patients with Lesch-Nyhan disease.[12] Phase III testing in heart surgery was stopped for futility.[1] No studies of acadesine for fat loss or appearance in healthy people were found.

Acadesine is on the WADA prohibited list, and a 2009 BMJ report cited by Wikipedia said WADA found evidence of its use by cyclists.[1] It is sold online as a research chemical, and is described as an exercise mimetic in online fitness communities.

card.summary: AMPK activator hyped as an exercise mimetic; no human fat-loss evidence, and banned in sport.

quick.overview:
Acadesine (AICAR) is a compound that activates AMPK, a cellular energy sensor. A 2008 mouse study reported endurance gains, and it is sold online as an exercise mimetic.

It was tested in humans for heart-surgery protection, not fat loss, and that trial stopped for futility.
quick.mechanism: It is converted inside cells to an AMP-like molecule that activates AMPK, raising fat oxidation and glucose uptake in muscle in animal studies.
quick.risks: It is not approved, and is on the WADA prohibited list. Human safety data for body-composition use are lacking.
